label: Some Simple Knot Invariants
notes: Open the lecture. Before the deep polynomial theory, several elementary invariants already distinguish many knots. The lecture surveys crossing number, tricolorability, the linking number for links, and the unknotting number, each a concrete quantity that captures a different facet of knottedness in a simple way.

label: Crossing Number
notes: Define the crossing number as the least number of crossings in any diagram of the knot. It is obviously an invariant and orders the knot tables, yet it is notoriously hard to compute because one must rule out all simpler diagrams. The unknot has crossing number zero and the trefoil three.

label: Tricolorability
notes: Introduce tricolorability: a knot is tricolorable if its arcs can be colored with three colors so that at every crossing the three meeting arcs are all equal or all different, using more than one color. This property is invariant under Reidemeister moves and instantly distinguishes the trefoil, which is tricolorable, from the unknot, which is not.

label: The Linking Number
notes: For a two-component link, define the linking number by counting signed crossings between the two components and halving. It measures how many times one component wraps around the other and is invariant under Reidemeister moves. The Hopf link has linking number one, certifying that its two circles cannot be pulled apart.

label: The Unknotting Number
notes: Define the unknotting number as the minimum number of crossing changes, switching over to under, needed to turn the knot into the unknot. Every knot can be undone by enough switches, so this is well defined. It is a genuine measure of complexity but, like crossing number, is difficult to compute exactly.

label: Recap
notes: Close the lecture. Crossing number, tricolorability, the linking number, and the unknotting number are simple invariants that already separate many knots and links. Each is elementary yet captures real information, and tricolorability foreshadows the algebraic colorings behind deeper invariants. The next lecture introduces the Kauffman bracket.
